Part 27: The Situation in China — I. Activities of the Japanese Military Forces; II. Japanese Naval Operations in the Third Year of the China AffairTokyo Gazette, February, 1940, pp. 319-325

p. 319

THE SITUATION IN CHINA

I

ACTIVITIES OF THE JAPANESE MILITARY FORCES

BUREAU OF INFORMATION, WAR DEPARTMENT

The Chinese "Winter Offensive"

The so-called Chinese April and September offensives ended in miserable failures before our vigorous counter-attacks. In December, 1939, the Chinese forces launched their "winter offensive," which kept our troops busy.

Generally speaking, it must be noted that the European War has exercised adverse effects on the Chiang Kai-shek régime, while our campaign near Pakhoi has added to the difficulty of the Chungking Government in securing war supplies from abroad. In addition to which, the movement by Wang Ching-wei and his followers for the establishment of a new Central Government in China, which has been achieving steady progress during 1939, has induced, not only leaders of the Chungking Government, but the Chinese masses, to pay more attention to peace. This serious turn of the situation, both at home and abroad, made Chiang Kai-shek resort to a "winter offensive" for the benefit of home and foreign consumption. The new operations, apparently, were planned systematically, with the Yangtze front as the main centre of activities and with a considerable force mobilized.

1. The Front North of the Yangtze

In the Singyang sector, fighting became very brisk around December 10. Two divisions of the Chinese forces were routed near Yanghaochen on December 14, while a force of similar strength was driven north by our troops near Changtaikwan three days later.

In the Suehsin, Anlu, Kiukowchen, Sientaochen and Anking sectors, fairly strong forces attacked us between the 12 and 22 December but were in every case repulsed despite heavy reinforcements which they had summoned.

2. The Front South of the Yangtze

In the Yochow, Tungcheng, Tsingyang and Wuning sectors, all Chinese moves between the 16 and 24 December ended in failure, requiring their immediate withdrawal before our counter-attacks, while heavy losses were inflicted on them in the Tsingan, Fengsin, Nanchang and Tsingyang sectors.

p. 320

3. The North China Front

That section of the Peking-Hankow Railway between Sinsiang and Changte, in Northern Honan Province, was tampered with by Chinese troops, but the damage was slight. Necessary repairs were immediately made by our railway corps so that the train service was not interrupted.

In the South Shansi sector, along the Tatung-Puchow railway, a severe blow was dealt the Chinese at Kianghsien and Hotsin resulting in their fleeing to the Tahsing Mountains, dividing Shansi from Honan Province. At Luan, in South-East Shansi, no activity was recorded.

4. The Inner Mongolia Front

Chinese troops, about one division strong, attacked Paotow, the western terminus of the Peking-Suiyuan Railway on the morning of December 20, but were driven away with heavy losses on the afternoon of December 23.

5. The South China Front

The Chinese armies in South China had been preparing a winter offensive since the end of November, but met with a large-scale counter-attack by our troops and were dislodged from their positions in the mountainous area east of the North River. We made a sweeping drive northward and destroyed the enemy bases at Yungyun, Sanhwachen and Yingtak, thus dealing the armies under General Yu Han-mou a crushing blow. Mopping-up operations succeeded this gain.

It is ascertained that the Chinese troops confronting us in that region, up to January 1, numbered some 100,000 strong. They lost about 15,000 killed and 2,000 prisoners. Japanese booty included 8 trench-mortars, 20 heavy machine-guns, 95 light machine-guns, 3 anti-aircraft guns, 2,600 rifles, 9,000,000 rounds of ammunition and 4,000,000 shells.

A push along the Canton-Hankow Railway succeeded in driving the enemy from Yinchanyao and Yuntam, some 60 kilometres north of Canton, between December 1 and 21 and in capturing Yintak late December 30.

A detachment, moving from Tsungfa, routed a division of Chinese troops to the northeast of that town on December 22, reaching Leungkowhu on December 25 and Lutienhu on December 27.

Another column from Tsengshing dislodged two divisions of Chinese troops from Yunghanhu on December 17 and advanced to Meikang late December 26. Reducing Yungyun, this column, on December 31, occupied Sanhwachen, headquarters of General Yu Han-mou, Commander-in-chief of the Chinese armies in Kwangtung Province for the past year.

The Kwangsi Campaign

Nanning, the former capital of Kwangsi Province, was cleared of Chinese troops on November 26, 1939, entry having been effected two days previous to that. Out of a garrison of 6,000 men 2,200 were killed. Our casualties were about 200 killed and wounded, and our booty included 4 artillery pieces, 6 machine-guns, 48 light machine-guns and 264 rifles.

p. 321

Part of these retreating troops massed along the line connecting Pinyang, Yungshun and Luowhan, some 60 kilometres east of Nanning, and part concentrated in a mountainous area near Wuming. Here they reorganized themselves for a counter-attack. Mopping-up operations against Chinese regular forces and guerillas took place in Western Kwangtung and Southern Kwangsi Provinces.

1. The Nanning Sector

A strong position on a height near Patang, about 40 kilometres northeast of Nanning, was taken by us on December 3, the enemy leaving behind some 500 dead, 1 heavy machine-gun and 75 rifles. We made 5 prisoners. Our losses were 9 killed and 61 injured.

Another detachment operated from the night of November 30 against Takaofeng, and dealt 3,000 enemy troops a crushing blow. They lost 1,062 killed and 8 prisoners. Booty included 7 howitzers, 5 heavy machine-guns, 7 light machine-guns, 285 rifles and 8 telephones. Our casualties were 12 killed and 47 injured.

The defeated Chinese troops, on December 4, massed along a line north of Chiutang, some 45 kilometres northeast of Nanning. With the arrival of reinforcements, they started another attack, on December 18, along the Pinyang-Nanning highway. They were some seven divisions strong and well-equipped with artillery and tanks. On the evening of December 21, several enemy planes appeared near Chiutang and attacked our positions but did no damage. Japanese detachments dashed from Nanning to Chiutang to encircle the Chinese forces.

Chinese guerillas were active at Wutsunhu, Tangpaohu, Tatanghu and other places, between 30 and 40 kilometres south of Nanning.

In the morning of December 25, three Chinese planes bombed Nanning airfield but did no damage.

The Chinese troops engaged around Nanning were 10 divisions strong.

2. The Yamchow Sector

At noon, December 7, a detachment advanced to Niukanghsu, about 20 kilometres northeast of Yamchow, and dislodged the enemy from along the line between Pingkihsu and Tsingtanghsu, besides defeating them at Hsiaotunghsu. The Chinese left some 400 dead. Our casualties were 10 killed and 12 wounded.

3. The Lungchow Sector

After their occupation of Nanning, our forces drove upon Lungchow, the southwestern extremity of Kwangsi Province, in order to cut off the arms supply route from French Indo-China. Dislodging a small number of Chinese troops holding Tunhsu and Ningming, and repairing the roads and bridges which had been destroyed, they occupied Lungchow and Chennankwan on the evening of December 21.

Japanese booty at Lungchow included 27,000 gallons of gasoline, 6,500 gallons of heavy oil, 16,000 kilogrammes of lead, 5,000 brass bars, and

p. 322

large quantities of arms and ammunition. That taken at Chennankwan, awaits further investigation. From this, it is evident that Lungchow and Chennankwan were important centres on the route of arms-supply to the Chiang Kai-shek Government from French Indo-China.

p. 323

II

JAPANESE NAVAL OPERATIONS IN THE THIRD YEAR OF THE CHINA AFFAIR

PUBLICITY BUREAU, NAVY DEPARTMENT

CONTENDING against very inclement weather, our warships carried out a blockade of the China coast including Shantung, Kiangsu, Chekiang, Fukien and Kwangtung Provinces, thus cutting off the sea-routes of arms supply to the Chiang Kai-shek régime. Key points on the China coast have been occupied by our naval forces, while fleets of troop transports have been successfully escorted by our warships, which also covered landing operations of military units effectively.

Inland waters in China, including the Yangtze, Pearl, Kwan, Sheyang and other rivers, and Poyang and other lakes, have been put under our control, mines swept, booms and other obstructions removed, while remnants of the Chinese troops and guerillas which infested the shores have been suppressed. Our lines of communication along these channels have been thus efficiently maintained.

The naval air force has effectively co-operated in, and made substantial contributions to the success of, operations started by warships, landing-parties and military units. It is also helping to break the enemy's resistance by daring attacks on military works and air bases in the rear of the Chinese lines.

Tightening of the Blockade: Our Navy has succeeded in effectively suspending Chinese shipping within the past two years with the avowed object of cutting off the arms supply to the Chiang Kai-shek régime from abroad by way of the sea. In view of the fact, however, that third-Power vessels provided the Chungking Government with war supplies by plying between foreign ports and Chinese ports not yet in our occupation, our Navy completely blockaded the following twelve ports from late in June to the middle of September: Wenchow, Foochow, Chuanchow, Tungshan, Chaoan, Swabue, Hinghwa, Santuao, Loyuan, Shating, Haimen and Meichow.

Hainan Campaign: On February 10, 1939, the Japanese Navy not only covered the landing of military units on the shore of Tengmai Bay, in the north of Hainan Island, but co-operated with the troops in occupying Hoihow (Haikow) and Kiungchow. On February 14, a naval force landed near Samah Port and occupied the area adjoining. Order has been restored over the island, all enemy troops and guerillas having been driven out.

The Clean-up Campaign in Haichow and Hwaiyin Districts: In co-operation with the military clean-up campaign in Haichow and Hwaiyin areas, our naval force covered the landing operations and, on February 28, opened up

p. 324

the Kwan River which flows into Siangshui Port; while the Sheyang River, which empties into Fowning, and the Linhung River, which flows into Haichow, were opened to traffic on March 8 and 11 respectively.

Nanchang Campaign: In concert with the military drive on Nanchang, capital of Kiangsi Province, naval detachments sailed up Lake Poyang and the Siushui and Wushui Rivers. Despite the inclement weather, they succeeded in opening a waterway as far as Nanchang on April 3. Some warships reached Shengmeichieh.

Swatow Campaign: On June 21, 1939, a naval detachment covered the landing operations of military units at the mouth of the Siki River, opening up the port of Swatow the same day.

Occupation of the Chusan Islands: From May 21 to July 17, naval detachments occupied Taishan and other scores of islands belonging to this group.

The Siangkiang Campaign: On September 23, 1939, a naval detachment covered the military landing near Yingtien successfully, opening up the Siangkiang River for a distance of 40 miles, disposing of 560 mines and removing booms.

The Clean-up Campaign in the Kaoyu Lake District: In concert with the military clean-up campaign in Kaoyu and Paoying areas, the naval detachment succeeded in opening the waterway to Paoying on October 3, to Chiangchiapa on October 4 and to Tienchang on October 7.

The Drive on Chungshanhsien: In co-operation with military units, our men occupied Chungshanhsien on October 7, withdrawing 3 days later, after defeating the enemy.

Safeguarding of the Waterways on the Yangtze and Pearl Rivers: The Japanese naval force is making strenuous efforts to safeguard the waterways on the Yangtze and Pearl Rivers which form the major lines of communication for the operations in Central and South China.

Remnants of the Chinese troops are still active along the lower reaches of the Yangtze. Our shipping is bombarded by enemy artillery at one or two points at irregular intervals, but these attacks are invariably silenced.

The Nanning Campaign: On November 15, warships effectively covered the landing operations of military units on the shores of Yamchow Bay. A base for sea-planes was also established.

Activities of the Naval Air Force

Our naval air force has made close co-operation with the operations of warships, landing parties and military units, achieving signal successes. In the Nanning campaign, the naval-air units efficiently co-operated with the ground forces. In doing so, however, they strictly adhered to the principle of respecting the rights and interests of third Powers, frequently in the face of certain disadvantages and sacrifices.

Attacks on the Arms-supply Routes in Kwangsi Province: While attacking and destroying Chinese military establishments all over China, the naval air-units have been intensifying their attacks on the arms-supply routes from French Indo-China through Kwangsi Province via Nanning, Liuchow and Kweilin.

Attacks on Hinterland Points: Points in the hinterland, to which the

p. 325

Japanese naval air force has paid special attention, are Mengtze on the Haiphong-Yunnanfu railway in Southeastern Yunnan Province, Kunming, capital of Yunnan Province, Luchow in Southern Szechuan Province, Chengtu, capital of Szechuan Province, Suining in Central Szechuan Province, Sian, capital of Shensi Province, Lanchow, capital of Kansu Province, and Chungking, seat of the Chiang Kai-shek Government. These points have been attacked by naval air-units from time to time in order to destroy the Chinese air force and to obliterate their military establishments. The naval air force has raided Chungking twenty times, destroying government buildings and military works.

Results of the Operations of the Naval Forces

Up to December 20, 1939, the naval forces, including the air arm, have inflicted the following losses on the Chinese:

Part 28: The Situation in China — I. Results of the Military Operations in the 12 Months following the Fall of Hankow; II. Activities of the Imperial Naval Air ForceTokyo Gazette, March, 1940, pp. 371-374

p. 371

THE SITUATION IN CHINA

I

RESULTS OF THE MILITARY OPERATIONS IN THE 12 MONTHS FOLLOWING THE FALL OF HANKOW

BUREAU OF INFORMATION, WAR DEPARTMENT

The Japanese expeditionary forces in North, Central and South China have achieved remarkable successes in cleaning up remnants of the Chinese troops and guerillas and maintaining peace and order along a fighting line extending over 4,000 kilometres, since the time of the capture in October, 1938, of the three Wuhan cities of Hankow, Wuchang and Hanyang. On December 28, 1939, the Army section of the General Headquarters gave out a communique reviewing the results of the major campaigns in the year following the fall of Hankow.

This may be summarized in the table below:

p. 372

In the meantime, Chiang Kai-shek launched the so-called April, July and September offensives against our positions with the dual purpose of stimulating Chinese morale and demonstrating to the pro-Chiang foreign Powers that his armies still possessed good fighting spirit and ability. The offensives, however, were no more than large-scale guerilla warfare, and collapsed before vigorous Japanese counter-attacks.

In those three offensives, we engaged Chinese troops numerically 1,114,300 strong. They lost 94,358 dead in addition to 6,704 prisoners. Japanese booty included 7 mountain-guns, 553 native-made guns, 61 mortars, 1 rapid-firer, 37 trench-mortars, 120 heavy machine-guns 322 light machine-guns and 12,148 rifles.

The Japanese expeditionary forces in North, Central and South China suffered some 27,000 killed up to November, 1939.

Activities of the Military Air Force

A communique, issued on December 29, 1939, by the Army Section of General Headquarters gives the following information on the activities of the military air force:

(1) Our air force shot down 330 Chinese planes and destroyed another 160 on the ground since the outbreak of the China affair.

p. 373

In the latter half of 1939, the Japanese military raiders have practically gone unchallenged by the enemy.

No official information was available up to time of going to press as to the results of the joint attacks by the Army and Navy air forces on Lanchow, capital of Kansu Province, on December 26, 27 and 28, 1939.

(2) In the Nomonhan incident, the Japanese military air force brought down 1,340 Soviet planes and destroyed another 520 on the ground.

(3) The Japanese military air force has lost 188 planes since the beginning of the China affair.

p. 374

II

ACTIVITIES OF THE IMPERIAL NAVAL AIR FORCE

PUBLICITY BUREAU, NAVY DEPARTMENT

With the China affair entering its fourth year, the three arms of the Japanese forces, land, sea and air, are making further advance in China.

The Japanese Naval Air Force, on New Year's Day, conducted large-scale operations against the Chinese troops and military establishments, bombing Nanking, capital of Kwangsi Province and the south bank of the Yangtze River. A row of Chinese military depots was destroyed.

On January 2, Central Hunan Province was visited by naval air-units under Lieutenant-Commander Awano, which raided Paoking (Shaoyang) repeatedly, and Hengyang, destroying the air bases. The Chinese offered no resistance to these aerial attacks.

The same morning, another flight led by Lieutenant-Commander Shimada, visited Southern Hunan Province and accounted for a number of enemy planes.

In North China, our naval air-units on January 2 visited Chingchihchen, west of Kaomi, along the Shantung Railway, and Siangchow-chen, on the Wei River, acting in concert with the landing party. On January 3 and 7, sustained attacks were made on several enemy bases in Shantung Province.

A surprise attack on Kweilin, capital of Kwangsi Province, was delivered on January 10 and 23 Chinese planes destroyed.

An aerial battle with some 40 Chinese planes took place over Liuchow, after which the air-field at Kweilin was again bombed and nine planes burned.

In South China, the Japanese military and naval forces, in close co-operation, achieved remarkable results ever since the campaign near Pakhoi was opened. Enemy concentrations were attacked and the cutting of the Yunnan Railway, route of the arms supply to the Chungking Government from French Indo-China, became the main objective. Kweilin, Liuchow, Mengtze and other enemy bases likewise received the attention of our airmen.

In this campaign, our naval air force accounted for no less than 55 Chinese planes between December 22 and January 10, thus nullifying the efforts of the Chungking Government to reorganize their air force with Kunming, capital of Yunnan Province, and Mengtze, to the southeast and a strategic point on the Yunnan Railway, as bases. This reorganization had been ordered by Chiang Kai-shek as part of that "winter offensive" which collapsed before our vigorous counter-attacks.

Part 29: The Situation in China (Activities of the Japanese Military Forces; Forces of the Imperial Navy in Action)Tokyo Gazette, April, 1940, pp. 412-416

p. 412

The Situation in China

I. Activities of the Japanese Military Forces

Bureau of Information, War Department

The Nanning Campaign

Movements of the Chinese troops and Topography of the Nanning area

The Chinese troops after being compelled to abandon Nanning on November 14 last, mostly retreated to the northeast of that city. With reinforcements from Kweilin and Hengyang, in Hunan Province, they resumed their offensive in December, and by the middle of the month were some twenty divisions strong with tanks and air units. They repeatedly attacked our lines of communication between Yamchow and Nanning, while exerting the greatest pressure on Nanning itself. The mountainous character of this part of Kwangsi Province however renders any counter-offensive extremely difficult.

Development of the Campaign

The Japanese forces entrenched themselves at Taikaoai and Chiutang, south of Pinyang, to lure the enemy and then surround them by a detour via the Yukiang River. They succeeded in outflanking the enemy from Wingshun (Yungshun), and from February 1, the encircling movement steadily tightened.

Meanwhile, certain Japanese units at Chiutang and Kunlunkwan were surrounded by Chinese troops and it was in coming to their aid that Major-General Nakamura met a heroic death on December 25.

February 2. The Miyamori, Wase, Nagakawa, Shiroki, Sumida, Miki and Hayashi detachments, operating in the sector near Chiutang to the south, pressed the enemy back to a mountainous district northwest of the town, and contacting the outflanking troops mentioned higher up, entrapped twenty divisions of the enemy who, in the ensuing confusion, stampeded to Tsienkiang, Lungshan and Wuming.

Results of the Campaign

The results of the campaign were as follows :

(a) The Chinese troops, some 35 divisions strong including 5 heavy and 10 field and mountain artillery battalions with one anti-tank unit, Lost 46,800 killed and 2,500 prisoners. The wounded were estimated at no less than 80,000.

(b) Japanese booty included 25 field and mountain guns, 16 rapid-firers, 68 trench-mortars, 125 grenade catapults, 110 heavy and 544 light machine-guns, 9,600 rifles, 19 tanks, 6 armoured cars, 63 motor-cars and

p. 413

8 side-cars. We suffered 205 killed and 785 wounded.

Statement of the Chief of the Press Section of the Army Department of the Imperial Headquarters

With regard to the Nanning campaign, the chief of the Press Section of the Army Department of the Imperial Headquarters on February 3 gave out the following statement :

"A coup-de-grâce has been dealt the so-called 'winter offensive' of Chiang Kai-shek by a decisive battle fought near Nanning, a key point of the arms-supply route for the Chungking Government. This has further stimulated the peace desire among the Chinese masses, and furthered the proposed establishment of a new central Government of China under Wang Ching-wei."

He went on to describe the operations, details of which appear in the opening chapter.

The Clean-up Campaign West of Paotow

General Situation

The Chinese armies under General Ma Chan-shan, Han Hsi-how, and Fu Tso-i, together with the guerillas under General Ho Chu-kuo, were active in the area around Paotow, western terminus of the Peking-Suiyuan Railway. A clean-up campaign was launched against them on January 20 by the Japanese forces patrolling the district.

Progress of the Campaign

From January 21 to January 25, mopping-up operations were carried out in the Ordos desert, south of the Yellow River, against the enemy some 2,000 strong. Anpeh and Changyatien, both west of Paotow, were the starting-points of attacks directed upon Wuyuan and Wuchen, on January 31. Capturing Wanhochang, the Japanese advanced to Wuyuan on February 3.

Moving south, they took Tunghingtang, and heavily defeating troops under Generals Men Ping-yueh and Shin Yu-shan, they reached Linho and Shanpa on February 5.

In Shantung Peninsula

General Situation

The Tsingtao Campaign of 1904 and later, the Japanese expedition to Tsinan, had taught the people of Shantung Province the value of the Japanese military. This accounts for the latter's success in maintaining peace and order in the Shantung peninsula since the outbreak of the China Affair. However, the eastern extremity of the peninsula, which had not known Japanese occupation, had for long been used by Chinese Communist and Kuomintang troops as well as irregulars as bases for operations against the

p. 414

law-abiding populace. Early in February military and naval forces were sent against them. Serious difficulties attended these operations because of the mountainous nature of the country, the muddy roads and cold and inclement weather.

Movements of the Chinese Troops

About 20,000 Chinese troops and irregulars overran Eastern Shantung. The Shantung column of the Communist 8th Route Army, some 2,000 strong, was moreover active, with Chaoyuan, south of Lungkow, as its base. There were regular troops or guerilla forces in Penglai prefecture and the Laiyang, Tsihsia and Tsimo districts ; also in the Fushan, Tengchow and Hwanghsien, Wenteng and Yungcheng districts.

Progress of the Campaign

The Japanese campaign was aimed at cornering these elements within the tip of the Shantung peninsula.

Our military forces drove from Lunghow and Piehshan on February 7, the Yamazaki, Akimoto, Ide and Oku detachments reaching the Chefoo-Haiyan line on February 13. Wenteng, the major base of enemy operations, was occupied on February 18, and Yungcheng three days later. Meanwhile the Japanese North China fleet tightened the blockade along the Shantung coast. On February 18, Shihtao, a strategically important port at the south-eastern extremity of the peninsula, was occupied by a naval detachment which captured Hwangshantsi, some 20 kilometres to the northwest, on February 19. This movement cut off the southern retreat of the enemy.

The mopping-up campaign in the peninsula was successfully concluded within a fortnight of its start.

Results of the Campaign

Between February 1 and February 21, 59 engagements with the enemy, whose numbers were estimated at 15,000, had taken place. They lost some 1,200 killed and 80 prisoners. Booty included about 400 rifles.

p. 415

The Situation in China

II. Forces of the Imperial Navy in Action

Publicity Bureau, Navy Department

Activities of the Japanese naval air force in South China were seriously hampered by unfavourable weather since late in January. This allowed the Chungking Government time to repair the Yunnan Railway, its most important arms-supply route from abroad, which had been paralysed by successive aerial attacks.

On February 1, however, we carried out bombing operations against Mengtze, in Yunnan Province. Naval air-units led by Lieut.-Commander Mihara reached Mengtze, after a difficult passage. The Yunnan Railway was bombed at the bridge near Mengtze, and again its service paralysed. Much resistance however was encountered from the ground defences of the enemy.

Meanwhile other units visited Kwangsi Province and operated in concert with the ground forces.

The press section of the Japanese fleet in South China waters issued the following statement regarding the attack carried out by the naval air-units on the Yunnan Railway, on February 2 :

"On February 1, a big naval air detachment, in formation, commanded by Lieut.-Commander Mihara, carried out bombing operations against the Yunnan Railway, the only arms-supply route left to the Chungking Government, in the face of inclement weather and strong enemy opposition from the ground and air. The Chinese planes were easily repulsed. Heavy damage was inflicted on the railway. We suffered no losses."

Active Part Played by the Naval Force in the Clean-up Campaign in Eastern Shantung Province

The Japanese military and naval forces in North China started a mopping-up campaign against the remnants of Chinese troops in Eastern Shantung Province early in February.

On February 7, our military forces, from Langkow, Chaoyuan, Jihchwang, Lingshanchieh and Puchutientze closed in upon the remnants of the enemy, some 20,000 strong, which overran Eastern Shantung.

Taking advantage of the unique topography, these troops were steadily cornered into the extremity of the peninsula. In the meantime, the Japanese Navy enforced a ban on shipping including the junk traffic between Weihaiwei and Tsingtao. The blockade was in every way effective.

The mopping-up campaign, jointly carried out with the military forces, was participated in by the air-units. Much hardship was experienced, because of the extreme cold and the bad weather.

p. 416

The press section of the Japanese fleet in North China waters on February 19 gave out the following communique :

"(1) Several naval planes early on the morning of February 18 participated in the attack on Shitao, covering the landing operations of our blue-jackets.

"(2) At the same time, our warships bombarded the enemy positions in the rear, cutting off their retreat.

"(3) The defeated enemy troops attempted to flee into the mountainous district north of Shihtao. The Chinese population in the port welcomed our men upon their entry.

Peace and order is fast returning in this region."

February 20, the Japanese resident naval officer Tanimoto at Tsingtao issued a statement :

"Since the morning of February 20, a clean-up campaign against the remnants of Chinese troops, is being undertaken and the coast districts carefully kept under surveillance.

"Midway between Weihaiwei and Chefoo was bombarded and heavy damage inflicted on the enemy.

"The main body of the Japanese fleet is anchored off Shihmen Port where mopping-up operations are being directed against all stragglers.

"We captured 41 rifles, 2 revolvers, and about 4,000 rounds of ammunition."

Part 30: The Situation in China — Clean-up Campaign in the Wuyuan SectorTokyo Gazette, May, 1940, pp. 458

p. 458

The Situation in China

Clean-up Campaign in the Wuyuan Sector

Bureau of Information, War Department

As a sequel to the Japanese mopping-up operations conducted from late in January till early in February this year, the Chinese troops under General Fu Tso-i abandoned Wuyuan, some 250 kilometres northwest of Paotow, western terminus of the Peking-Suiyuan Railway, and fled northwest into Mongolia where they reorganized themselves at Linho, Shanpa and points in the Ordos plain.

In an attempt to recapture Wuyuan, they launched another attack, with four divisions of the 35th Army, upon the town at dawn on March 21, likewise moving against Nanniupa, some 15 kilometres south of Wuyuan, and various points along the north bank of the Wuchiaho River.

The Wuyuan garrison was composed mostly of native troops of the Federated Autonomous Government of Mongolia, with a sprinkling of Japanese.

The defenders being greatly outnumbered, Japanese reinforcements from Paotow, western terminus of the Peking-Suiyuan Railway, were hurriedly dispatched to their relief. Cooperating with the Yamaguchi air detachment, the relief column reached Taineichiao, about 8 kilometres north of Wuyuan, on the evening of March 22, and 3 days later, effected a crossing of the Wuchiaho River some 10 kilometres northeast of Wuyuan. Defeated, the Chinese forces fled to the west and south.

The Chinese lost some 500 dead, and the material captured from them included 2 mountain guns, 30 heavy machine-guns of Czecho-Slovakian make, with large quantities of arms and ammunition. We suffered 10 killed and 80 wounded ; while 33 Japanese residents of Wuyuan lost their lives.

Part 31: The Situation in China — The Han River Campaign; Activities of the Japanese Naval Air Force in ChinaTokyo Gazette, July, 1940, pp. 31-33

p. 31

The Situation in China

I. The Han River Campaign

Bureau of Information, War Department

The so-called Chinese winter offensive collapsed on all fronts about the end of January despite Chiang Kai-shek's contention that the Japanese army had lost its striking power. Chinese troops were defeated near Pinyang in Kwangsi Province, and also at Wuyuan, 250 kilometres northwest of Paotow, the western terminus of the Peking-Suiyuan Railway. Meanwhile, a new Central Government had been inaugurated at Nanking under the leadership of Wang Ching-wei, to which Japan is extending every assistance.

On April 17, a clean-up campaign in southeast Shansi against the 60,000 Chinese troops under General Wei Li-huang, was undertaken. Other operations in that province, involving about 180,000 of Chiang's forces, ended in the occupation of Tsehchow and other strategic towns.

In the area south of the Yangtze River, between Wuhu and Hukow, a mopping-up campaign was commenced on April 20. In order to safeguard navigation on that river, it was necessary to drive the Chinese out of Tsingyang, which movement was successfully executed by the end of April. To the northwest of Hankow, a general offensive against the enemy in the fifth war-zone took place early in May. Through difficult terrain, our forces reached the Piyuan-Tsaoyang-Luyinchen line, to the northeast of Tsaoyang, on May 7. The Shansi campaign had been undertaken primarily to restore peace and order, while operations on the south bank of the Yangtze and east of the Han River were conducted in order to break Chinese resistance and give the lie to Chungking's propaganda. The South Honan and North Hupeh operations in May were the largest we conducted this year, some 20 divisions of Chinese troops being entrapped near the Tangho River. Those that had set up bases in the Tahung and Tapieh mountain ranges, and had been reinforced by men from the armies under Tang En-po and Sun Lien-chung in the north and west and Chang Tzu-chung in the south—in all some 12 divisions strong—were successfully dealt with.

On May 19, the Japanese forces in the regions around Tsaoyang launched an attack along the entire front, shattering the Chinese resistance and decimating their troops.

Investigations into the results of the campaign have not been completed, but it is known that the Chinese forces lost 19,837 dead in addition to 730 prisoners up to May 17. Japanese booty included 1 anti-aircraft gun, 6 trench-mortars, 165 heavy machine-guns, 2,858 rifles and 124 automatic rifles. The figures would be considerably increased were the casualties sustained after May 19 included. The Japanese suffered only 411 killed.

p. 32

The Situation in China

II. Activities of the Japanese Naval Air Force in China

Publicity Bureau, Navy Department

Yunnan : Three Japanese naval air units, led by Lieut.-Commander Mihara, on April 4 raided Pingma on the Yukiang River in Kwangsi Province, destroying a munition dump and several fuel depots. Following repeated aerial attacks on the Yunnan Railway, main arms supply route of the Chungking Government, the traffic was directed to Kweichow and Szechwan Provinces via Pingma, so that this town acquired considerable military importance.

Japanese naval air detachments under Lieut.-Commander Mihara raided Paichai, 60 kilometres from the Indo-China border, on April 26, and damaged the Yunnan Railway bridge. This and previous attacks have resulted in a complete disruption of traffic by that route.

South China : On May 1, military establishments, some 150 motor-lorries, and an ammunition dump at Kweiyang, capital of Kweichow Province, were destroyed. On May 9, Kunming, capital of Yunnan Province, was bombed ; and on May 14, the important highway between that city and Kweiyang attacked.

Hunan : Japanese air units, commanded by Lieut.-Commander Shimada, on April 12 staged a surprise raid on the airfield at Chinkiang, on the western border of Hunan Province.

Chekiang : Three days later, the same group of fliers attacked Chinese air-bases at Lishui in Chekiang Province, Yushan and Shangjao (Kwangsin) in Kiangsi Province. Other air-units, led by Lieutenants Ikeda and Okuyama also visited Lishui and Shangjao (Kwangsin), severely damaging the railway. Lishui and Yushan were again raided on April 16, while the air-field and munition depots at Kian, in Central Kiangsi, were destroyed.

Szechwan : On April 2, air detachments made their appearance over Iping (Suchow), 110 kilometres west of Chungking, and effectively bombed the air-field, destroying a number of enemy planes.

At midnight, April 22, the Japanese naval air-force made its first large-scale attack on the Chinese air-bases around Chungking, particularly the one at Iping. On April 30, Kwangyangpa and Paishih were raided.

Crack units, under Lieut.-Commander Kurinohara, raided Chungking at midnight, April 24, The first unit, commanded by Lieutenant Ikeda, bombed military establishments at Suining, 90 miles northwest of that town, while the second and third units, under Lieutenants Nakamura and Okuyama raided Paishih, 10 miles southwest of Chungking. Chungking was again attacked on April 30, and the aerodrome at Siangshan bombed.

p. 33

Our fliers visited Chengtu, capital of Szechwan Province, on the night of May 18 damaging the airfields at Wenkiang, and Taipingsze. A surprise raid was made on Suining. On the nights of May 19, 20 and 21, other attacks being delivered on Chengtu, Iping (Suchow) Liangshan and Kwangyangpa.

Three Japanese air units made the biggest raid so far over Chungking at 3:30 p.m., May 26. One unit, led by Lieutenant Kotani, attacked Paishih, destroying munitions depots and six planes. Another flight, commanded by Lieutenant Sato, bombed Hsiaolungkan. The cadets' school, military establishments and the Futan University were wrecked and the Central Telegraph and Telephone Office destroyed. This was followed by other attacks on the two succeeding days during which Peipehsitsum, Tzetsikow and Futukwan, in the western suburbs of Chungking, were visited and the military arsenals and establishments of strategic value destroyed.

Development and Results of the Operations of the Japanese Naval Forces since the Beginning of the Year

Reviewing the development and results of the operations undertaken by the Japanese naval forces in China since the beginning of the year, the naval section of the Imperial Headquarters on May 31 gave out the following communiqué :

"In concert with the military forces, the Japanese naval forces in China have undertaken and successfully carried out various operations since the beginning of the year. The morale of the officers and men is high.

"The Japanese Navy has steadily tightened the blockade of the China coast. Smuggling by junks has been suppressed ; supply routes have been interrupted.

"In North China, the air arm co-operated with the military in a mopping-up campaign in Shantung Peninsula.

"While water communications on the Yangtze River have been securely maintained and the roving Chinese troops along the banks disseminated, mine-sweeping operations have been carried out by our ships and the waterways cleared of obstacles. Chungking, Chengtu, and other air-bases have been repeatedly bombed by our airmen.

"Similar operations on the Pearl River were attended with every success.

"Hainan Island has been successfully cleared of all remnants of enemy troops. This was carried out in conjunction with our land forces.

"From January to May 31, this year, the Japanese naval forces on the Yangtze and Pearl Rivers have disposed of 299 mines, of which 210 were in the former. This brings the total of mines disposed of since the beginning of the China Affair to 5,058.

"64 Chinese planes, of which 12 were unconfirmed, have been destroyed on the ground, and 69 (13 unconfirmed) brought down raising the total of such planes destroyed to 1,776 (260 unconfirmed) since the opening of hostilities."

Part 32: The Situation in China — Development of the Campaign West of the Han River; Activities of the Naval Air ForceTokyo Gazette, August, 1940, pp. 82-84

p. 82

The Situation in China

I. Development of the Campaign West of the Han River

Bureau of Information, War Department

1. General Situation

Some 20 divisions of Chinese troops were defeated by the Japanese forces in a three-day battle on the Paiho River, starting May 19, and driven into Northern Hupeh Province. East of the Han River from the Sinyang-Suihsien-Anlu line a clean-up campaign was initiated on May 1.

Meanwhile, operations against enemy positions to the west of that river, held by 350,000 men, were undertaken.

2. Crossing of the Han River

The Japanese forces crossed to the west bank of the Han River in two formations, one at Wangchiachai and Shangwangchiatsi southeast of Siangyang on the night of May 31, the other near Kiukowchen and Kwantowchienshih.

3. Development of the Campaign

Siangyang was taken early on June 1, after which the column swung south and reached the Chuanwantow-Liki-Losiangkwan line 4 days later to occupy Kingmen on June 6 and Tangyang on June 10 respectively.

The second column, more to the south, had meanwhile captured Chienyang on June 7 and Kingchow and Shasi the following day. Pushing further west, they occupied Ichang on the evening of June 11.

4. Significance of the Campaign

Surprise was the principal characteristic of the above movement so that the Chinese retired in confusion, leaving enormous quantities of arms and ammunition behind.

Between June 1 and June 12 they had lost 18,000 dead and 3,531 prisoners. While the Japanese suffered about 50 killed up to June 6. Booty included 44 artillery pieces, 150 machine-guns, 2,895 rifles, large quantities of ammunition, provisions and fodder.

p. 83

II. Activities of the Naval Air Force

Publicity Bureau, Navy Department

Sustained attacks are now being made on Chungking, seat of the Chiang Kai-shek Government, by the naval and military air forces, and on the Yunnan Railway, the new Southwestern highway connecting Kaobang in French Indo-China with Kweiyang, capital of Kweichow Province, and other trunk roads.

1. Cooperation with the Ground Forces

The Han River campaign started on May 1. On May 16, Japanese naval air-units based upon Hankow, visited Icheng, Taokow and Lihokow, destroying munition depots, piers and military craft.

In concert with the ground forces, operations were undertaken against Laokokow, headquarters of Li Tsung-jen, Commander-in-Chief of the Chinese forces, Siangyang and Hwanghotsi. The retreating enemy was pursued along the Paiho and Tangho rivers, and Neisiang, west of Nayang, and Maitsungchen were bombed. Siangyang was again raided on May 31.

A mopping-up campaign by our ground forces in which the naval air-unit participated was started east of Hukow, Kiangsi Province, late in May. Jaochow, Tsingyang and other places south of Hukow, enemy positions north of Hukow and bases east of Lake Panyang became targets of attack.

On May 27 several thousand Chinese troops which had surrounded the Japanese at Chihchow and Tuchang were dispersed.

Between June 1 and June 7 Wuanyen (west of Icheng), Kucheng (west of Siangyang), Nanchang, Kingmen, Shihkiaoyi, Kingchow, Ichang, Kiangkow and Shwanglienchang were visited in turn by our naval fliers and military objectives destroyed. Tanyang, Anfu and Tsikiho (east of Ichang) were also attacked. And strategic points including Tungshih, Kiangkow, Yuanshih, Chikkiang, Itu, Sungtze and Paiyang, between Ichang and Shasi, raided.

On June 9 and 10, Ichang and its neighbourhood was furiously bombed, and Chungking raided. On June 11 the Japanese military forces entered Ichang, but operations north and west of that city were continued.

2. Cooperation in the Blockade of the China Coast

On May 17, naval planes raided Wenchow, Santuao and Hinghwa and Foochow, and destroyed some of the highways out of these cities.

3. Attacks on the Yunnan Railway

At the end of the month Meilu, Suikai, Tinpak and Yangkiang on the

p. 84

Luichow peninsula received the attentions of our flying-units and the Yunnan Railway's service again paralysed.

Military works at Pingma, Kweiyang and Poseh and strategic positions in Northwestern Kwangsi Province were raided, including Fengyi, Lungshan, Hwaiyuan, Ishan, Nantain, Tesheng, Hochih and Kweishun.

4. Large-Scale Bombing Operations Against Chungking

Following attacks on the Chinese airbases in Szechuan Province late in April, the Japanese naval air force carried out a night raid on Wenkiang and Tapingsze near Chengtu and also on Suining on May 18. Several grounded planes were accounted for. Since May 19, Chungking, Chengtu, Ipin, Liangshan, and Suining have been raided repeatedly, and enemy planes to the number of 90 destroyed. This has meant a fatal blow to the Chinese air force.

From May 26 to 30 Chungking was subjected to a series of bombings of the military establishments, including an arsenal, government buildings, the wireless station, and the telegraph office. Six days later these were renewed by combined naval and military planes.

THE SITUATION IN CHINA

II

TIGHTENING OF THE BLOCKADE AGAINST CENTRAL AND SOUTH CHINA

PUBLICITY BUREAU, NAVY DEPARTMENT

In accordance with tightening of the blockade against the Central China coast, as proclaimed by Vice-Admiral Shimada, Commander-in-Chief of the Japanese fleet in China waters on July 15, a Japanese naval detachment started fresh operations in Hangchow Bay at dawn, July 16.

Reduction of the Paichi (Chenhai) and Changtiaotsui Forts: An attack on the Chenhai forts resulted in their complete occupation the same morning. The Changtiaotsui Fort was reduced the following day.

Occupation of Chenhai: These operations led to the occupation of Chenhai (outpost of Ningpo) on July 18, and of the islands which command the entrance.

Reduction of Chuanchow and Blockade of Hinghwa Bay: On July 17, a powerful Japanese fleet, in concert with the attack on Chuanchow, Fukien Province, moved in on Hinghwa Bay, 40 miles northeast of that town, and by sinking junks and placing obstructions in those waters, successfully closed the most important supply route in Fukien Province.

Attacks on Santuao and Shoutsun: On the morning of July 21, a landing-party gained a footing at Santuao against strong enemy resistance. The same afternoon, the Japanese entered Shoutsun, dismantled the Chinese military establishments and completely destroyed their lines of communication.

All these operations, which the Japanese Navy carried out in concert with the Naval air-units had for purpose the blockading of the outlet of the Chekiang-Kiangsi Railway, and the cutting-off of the supply route through these ports. Since the institution of the blockade more than ten foreign vessels were stopped and visited without incident. This tightening of the blockade against Central and South China ports has dealt a severe blow to the Chungking régime and the pro-Chiang foreign Powers.

III

AT SHANGHAI THREE YEARS AGO

PUBLICITY BUREAU, NAVY DEPARTMENT

August 13, is a day never to be forgotten by the Japanese nation, for that date three years ago, marked the opening of the Shanghai campaign, a

p. 121

unique and most thrilling one in the annals of war, following the provocative challenge of the Chinese army.

In greeting this third anniversary of the outbreak of the campaign, we recall with gratitude the bitter fighting waged by the Japanese landing party in its earlier stages and the subsequent close cooperation between the Japanese military and naval forces around Shanghai for more than 70 days. At the same time we pay a glowing tribute to those who lost their lives and to the sick and wounded for the valour they manifested. We who live and are well take this occasion to pledge our renewed efforts for the construction of a new order in East Asia on the altar of their sacrifice.

The campaign was marked by a lightning landing of Japanese forces in the international city in face of strong enemy resistance, and the coordinated activities of Japan's land and sea forces, with the naval and military air arms. It provided the occasion for originating tactical moves of no little consequence and furnished by the peculiarities which surrounded it valuable instructions and suggestions on the disposal of the China Affair itself.

Movements of the Japanese Navy Before and After the Outbreak of the Shanghai Campaign

The China Affair was the outcome of the outrageous, anti-Japanese policy, assiduously and systematically pursued by the Chiang Kai-shek régime in defiance of international justice over a period of many years. Anti-Japanism was the instrument by which that régime attempted to bring the whole of China under its control. Hatred of Japan was the guiding principle in the moral training of young China and of the Chinese Army—a line of education which is against all the principles of humanity. For years previous to the outbreak of hostilities military service was enforced among the people with this country as the hypothetical enemy, while rapid rearmament was pursued under the guidance of Western military experts. This bolstered the growing conceit of the Chinese military and led the nation to over-estimate its strength. The belittling of Japan's resources, and the spread of the war sentiments through the length and breadth of China could not but bring about the regrettable situation which resulted in open hostilities. Following the incident at Sian, capital of Shensi Province in December, 1936, when Chiang Kai-shek was made prisoner by Chang Hsueh-liang and his Communist colleagues, Chiang concluded an arrangement for cooperation between the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communists in offering resistance to Japan. And there and then a basic policy to carry on warfare against her neighbour was formulated by China's two opposing groups.

The rising storm of anti-Japanese hatred manifested itself in terroristic outbreaks in various parts of the republic.1

Nevertheless the officers and men of our China fleet exercised the greatest self-restraint upon all occasions. But the tide of anti-Japanese surged on to its climax in the Marco Polo Bridge incident of July 7, 1937. This was the signal for an open break between the two countries. The

1 For the full account of the outrageous incidents, see an article entitled "Significance of the North China Problem" in the August, 1937, issue of TOKYO GAZETTE.

p. 122

cause for all this was so deep-rooted that the spread of hostilities to Shanghai was inevitable, despite every effort on Japan's part to localize this incident. In August, the situation in Shanghai was suddenly aggravated. The Chinese army assumed a definitely provocative attitude, by constructing military works in the demilitarized zone along the perimeter of Shanghai, thus violating the truce agreement of 1932.

Japanese residents along the Yangtze River were advised to evacuate, their withdrawal commencing on August 1. By August 9 over 2,800 of them, under the protection of the Japanese Navy, were safely escorted to Shanghai from stations as far distant as 1,400 miles up that river. That same afternoon Naval Lieutenant Oyama and Warrant Officer Saito were butchered by Chinese troops, which added to the strain already imposed.

A settlement was sought, the Japanese landing party demanding the immediate withdrawal of the Chinese constabulary force from the demilitarized zone around Shanghai and the dismantling forthwith of the military works established on the perimeter. Instead of manifesting any sincerity in their negotiations, the Chinese military authorities became openly provocative steadily reinforcing their troops in and around Shanghai. At dawn, August 12, the Chinese 88th division arrived at the North Station by train and by lorry. Strong pillboxes which had been constructed in the compounds of the Greater Shanghai Municipal Government offices at Kiangwanchen and Chapei just outside the International Settlement were immediately manned and preparations made for action. The Japanese landing party, some 3,000 strong, thus found itself surrounded by forces ten times greater numerically which opened fire on them as the funeral services for the late Lieutenant Oyama and Warrant Officer Saito were being conducted at headquarters. In honour of the victims to Chinese atrocity, the Chinese army was brutal enough to fire upon the Japanese landing party, raising the curtain on the Shanghai campaign. It was the declared intention of the Chinese to annihilate not only the Japanese troops but also the 30,000 Japanese nationals then residing in Shanghai.

Crack units of the Japanese Navy were immediately despatched to reinforce their comrades as Vice-Admiral Ohkochi, Commander of the Japanese landing party, issued the historic order to his command, "Stand by and start fighting!" This was at 4:55 p.m., on August 13 when the Chinese troops opened fire upon the headquarters of the Japanese landing party. On August 23, our troops landed at Woosung against heavy odds as the Chinese forces had by this time swelled to 200,000. Signal credit is due to the Japanese Navy for the lightning sea and air operations by which victory at Shanghai was made possible.

Peculiarity of the Shanghai Campaign and British Obstructions

Spread of hostilities to Shanghai was inevitable, as it was part of the Chinese plan to engage Japan on that ideal battlefield for China. Through such a move Chiang hoped to involve those other Powers interested in that city in the conflict thus bringing about international complications

p. 123

which might result in intervention against Japan. Moreover, Nanking the seat of the Government and the military centre of the country, was but a few hours away with every water and land facility for concentrating large bodies of troops around China's principal port. The Chinese military likewise placed great reliance upon the costly fortifications which had been constructed in that vicinity during the preceding five years.

Our movements were greatly hampered by the peculiar conditions which obtained. In fact there were occasions when the Japanese defenders were exposed to most serious danger on this account. Some of these peculiarities we shall enumerate below:

1. Chinese Partisans or Plain-Clothes Soldiers

Chinese partisans or plain-clothes men were the ones who first fired on a sentry of the Japanese landing party on August 13, thus precipitating hostilities. Armed in every way, it was their mission to carry the conflict well into enemy lines and disturb peace in the rear. The international status of Shanghai, which allowed for the free movement of these irregulars who found the situation an ideal one for their activities, was one of the most serious problems with which our forces had to contend.

2. Street Fighting

Another difficulty was presented by street fighting with which the Japanese landing party was not unfamiliar and in which it had been carefully trained. Nonetheless that form of fighting which could be long-drawn and undecisive proved a considerable disadvantage to our troops, who found their actions greatly restricted. With heavy reserves to draw upon in case of need the Chinese could carry their defence from house to house, street to street, and to dislodge them necessitated the complete razing of all buildings in the town.

3. International Settlement and French Concession in Shanghai

Foreign Shanghai comprises an International Settlement and a French Concession, surrounded on all sides by Chinese territory—a condition which obtains nowhere else in the world, this afforded the Chinese troops tactical advantages of which they were not slow to make use. They took up strong positions for instance in Chapei (near the North Station), and attacks directed against them from the side were accompanied by the danger of shells falling within the International Settlement. Every inch of ground gained had to be bitterly contested and at the price of heavy sacrifice of Japanese lives.

The Chinese made the fullest use of the advantages provided them by the contiguity of their territory to the International Settlement and the French Concession, and ran their own defence lines right alongside those of the foreign troops guarding the Shanghai perimeter. This allowed for no inconsiderable assistance to them from across the border in devious ways, and instances of this aid, in which the British were directly concerned and which could not but prove obstructive to Japanese operations, are many.

In the opening aerial attack on the "Idzumo" Chinese bombs falling

p. 124

off their mark, severely damaged British-owned property close by. The British authorities requested that the "Idzumo" move away from her berth under threat of opening the Settlement barricades to the surrounding Chinese troops. The Chinese too were not debarred from access to tall buildings in the Settlement from which they were able to reconnoitre the Japanese lines. Our planes were fired at by anti-aircraft and machine-guns from the British-patrolled area. The besieging of the Joint Savings' Bank warehouse in which several hundred troops had barricaded themselves was another occasion for assistance and obstructive tactics. Provisions and water were supplied these troops from across the Settlement border and when, to evade capture, these men decided to make good their escape, the Settlement barricades were opened to assist them.

What took place at Shanghai was but the commencement of what went on during the whole campaign in China—the Chiang-aiding Powers treating the Settlements, which were in truth under the sovereign rule of China, as if they were their colonial possessions.

Japan is now engaged in the gigantic task of constructing a new order in Greater East Asia, with the same ideal as caused her to embark on the China Affair, namely the peace of the Orient. In recalling the Shanghai campaign we must renew our grim determination to cope efficiently with the current changes in the world by recognizing the gravity of the situation and establishing an intensive national defence structure on the basis of a new political structure.

Part 34: The Situation in ChinaTokyo Gazette, December, 1940, pp. 249-251

The Situation in China

Bureau of Information, War Department

p. 249

The large-scale clean-up campaign launched by the Japanese expeditionary forces since last April has dealt a heavy blow to the Chinese armies, upsetting reorganization plans launched by the Chinese armies early in July in an attempt to regain their fighting power.

Fearing that the Japanese forces might start a big offensive along the entire front in September or October, the Chinese armies attempted to obstruct Japanese troop movements and preparations for such an offensive by mobilizing guerilla activity in the rear of the Japanese positions. Sporadic engagements took place in various parts of China, including a Communist sortie in North China in the middle of August and activities by Chungking troops in southern Shansi Proyince [sic]. Otherwise, the China front has been relatively quiet.

The Chinese armies now are estimated at some 250 divisions, or about 2,000,000 men. Numerically each Chinese division is believed to have been replenished to its normal basic strength, but the equipment is barely sufficient to supply 20 or 30 per cent of the complement. In addition, a decided deterioration in the quality of recruits is manifested in frequent desertions and irregularities among the soldiers, as well as by low morale and slack discipline. The Chinese fighting spirit has declined seriously, although offers of heavy prizes and threats of severe punishment seem to serve somewhat to maintain it and some Chinese staff officers are still inflamed with vigorous anti-Japanese sentiments. But even the latter are limited to those who have never engaged Japanese troops, for Chinese officers and men usually lose the will to fight once they have borne the brunt of a Japanese attack.

The supply of munitions is an important factor in the enemy's capacity for resistance, and the major foreign supply routes to the Chungking régime have been almost completely blocked by the Japanese armed forces. It is true that a small quantity of munitions still trickles into the Chungking area over such routes as remain intact, but in general they are wholly inadequate for the needs of the Chinese armies. The Burma road, which Great Britain reopened after October 18, is said to be capable of accommodating only 1,500 tons of goods a month.

Chinese arsenals in the unoccupied areas apparently are capable

p. 250

of manufacturing ammunition in such quantity as to permit uninterrupted guerilla warfare on a small scale, but ordnance production is so poor that only small-calibre guns can be repaired.

In short, the fighting power of the Chinese armies has deteriorated remarkably, so that they are incapable of undertaking any offensive of the proportions of the battle of Hankow. It may be, however, that they will be capable of waging guerilla warfare for some time to come.

Activities of Chinese Communist Troops in North China

About 12,000 Chinese troops, comprising the 120th and 129th Divisions of the Eighth Route (Communist) Army and anti-Japanese university students, who established a base in the hinterlands of Shansi Province, attempted a sortie against the Tatung-Pukow Railway in northern Shansi Province, the railway between Shihkiachwang and Taiyuan, in Hopeh and Shansi Provinces, and the coal mines in Shansi Province on August 21. But the Japanese launched a counter-attack and they were completely repulsed with heavy losses by August 25. The Japanese forces also undertook a mopping-up campaign on October 11 against Chinese Communist troops which had been active in eastern Shansi Province and along the border of Hopeh Province.

The Central Front

In Central China, a punitive expedition was carried out against the newly organized Chinese 13th and 39th Divisions near Wuning, in Kiangsi Province, in August, while successful mopping-up campaigns were undertaken against the Chinese 76th Division near Hsiangan, in Anhwei Province, and also against Chinese troops which had been molesting the Hwainan Railway north of Luchow (Hofei), in central Anhwei Province. The biggest engagement during September took place in the lake region north of the Yangtze River, around Lake Kaoyu and Lake Hungtze, where the Japanese forces dealt the new Communist Fourth Army a severe blow after encircling them on September 5. In the lake region southeast of Tsienkiang, central Hupeh Province, mopping-up operations were started on October 13. Meanwhile a crushing attack was made against 20 Chinese divisions in an area extending from Wuhu to Hangchow and also south of Hangchow.

The South China Front

A portion of Chinese troops began activity in southwestern

p. 251

Kwangsi Province, bordering on French Indo-China, as a demonstration during August for both domestic and foreign effect. The Japanese forces in South China started operations on August 17 and dispersed Chinese troops near Shangsze, southwestern Kwansgi [sic], after inflicting heavy losses. Also on August 17, combined army and naval air forces swooped down upon Paoki, a strategic point on the northwestern or Red route on the western border of Shensi Province and effectively bombed military targets there. On August 19, military and naval air forces began joint attacks on Chungking for two consecutive days, scoring direct hits on military targets.

In September, Japanese army and navy forces, in conjunction with the Chinese constabulary, undertook a successful clean-up campaign against about 1,000 Chinese, remnants of hostile forces, on Hainan Island. This campaign is being continued in the interior of the island.

Japanese operations have been facilitated greatly by an accord concluded on September 22 between Japan and France, permitting Japanese armed forces to enter French Indo-China and to establish military and aviation bases there. This has made it possible for Japanese troops to withdraw from Nanning, former capital of Kwangsi Province, which had been occupied primarily to cut off supplies to the Chungking régime by way of French Indo-China through Yunnan and Kwangsi Provinces. Crack units of the Japanese army and navy air forces entered the air field at Hanoi on October 5, thus establishing a position from which to bomb effectively the Burma-Yunnan road, which was reopened to traffic on October 18.

Part 35: The Situation in China: Activities of the Imperial Naval Air ForceTokyo Gazette, January, 1941, pp. 289-291

The Situation in China: Activities of the Imperial Naval Air Force

Board of Information

p. 289

Before expiration of the three-month agreement between Japan and Great Britain, dating from July 17 and providing for the suspension of traffic in war materials along the Burma-Yunnan Road, Sir Robert Craigie, the British Ambassador, called on Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka on the morning of October 8 and informed him that the British Government could not see its way clear for a renewal of the agreement. The British communication appears to have been a manifest reaction to the conclusion of the Three-Power Agreement between Japan, Germany and Italy which was reached on September 27. It also may have been closely related to the 25,000,000 dollar loan granted to the Chiang Kai-shek régime by the United States Government on the eve of the conclusion of the Japan-Germany-Italy pact. These Anglo-American measures evidently had a common motive for assisting the Chungking régime and thwarting Japan's military operations in China. Be that as it may, Japan made a tacit reply to the reopening of the Burma Road by bombing and disrupting it.

The Burma Road Under Survey

The so-called Burma Road covers a distance of 1,146 kilometres from Rangoon, capital of Burma, to Kunming (Yunnan-fu), capital of Yunnan Province in China. About 85 per cent of the entire route lies within Yunnan Province and a one-way trip over the distance takes eight days. Construction of the road was started in 1937 and was completed eighteen months later, in 1938, at a cost of 200,000,000 yuan by 200,000 labourers.

That portion of the Burma Road lying within Yunnan Province is divided into two sections for administrative purposes, one extending from Kunming to Shengpei and the western section extending from Shengpei to Yenting. These two sections are subdivided into seven smaller sections. West of Siakwan, the road is generally impassable during the rainy season because of frequent landslides. In addition, there are more than 370 bridges along the entire route, of which only 10 are of modern type. East of Siakwan there are two big bridges, both old ones, and west of Siakwan there are six modern

p. 290

bridges. The most noted are those at Nuchiang (Hweitung), Yungping and Shengpei.

The Hweitung Bridge spans the rapids of the Nuchiang (Nu River), near the town of Luchiang, consisting of some 300 houses. The bridge has been rebuilt and re-enforced so that it can uphold trucks carrying up to three tons. The Yungping span is a suspension bridge over a rapid tributary of the Mekong River. Broader than the Hweitung Bridge and rebuilt on a modern foundation, it can support trucks carrying a load of five and a half tons. The Chinese Communications Ministry spent an enormous sum of money in constructing a suspension draw-bridge of the most modern type and it is guarded by scores of soldiers and anti-aircraft batteries even in peace-time. The Shengpei Bridge is not a suspension bridge and is surfaced with wood.

The Burma Road has two large bridges east of Siakwan, one in the western suburb of Hsiangyun and the other outside the eastern gate of Tsuyung. There is a relatively large bridge half-way between Hsiangyun and Tsuyung, in addition to about 90 medium-sized bridges and 288 smaller ones. All important bridges are well guarded and armed with anti-aircraft guns. There are repair facilities at important points along the road.

Until September, 1940, less than 200 trucks plied the Burma Road. Wireless service between Kunming and Rangoon was inaugurated on August 15, 1940, and the Burma Road offices in Kunming are connected with sectional offices by wireless and telephone.

There is a large repair garage in Kunming and smaller ones at Tali and Yenting.

Japanese Naval Air Arm Cuts Off Burma Route

On October 18, 1940, the very day on which Great Britain reopened the Burma Route, crack units of the Japanese naval air force swooped down on the road near the border of Yunnan Province and scored direct hits on a bridge spanning a gorge, seriously damaging it. The same day another powerful detachment of planes visited Kokiu, about 10 kilometres west of Mengtze, and effectively bombed a tin refinery there. Dense clouds hovering over the border area that day offered difficulty to the Japanese raiders, obscuring their targets, but a second bombing of the Burma Road was carried out on October 20 with satisfactory results against important bridges. Kokiu was raided again the same day, when Japanese naval planes attacked a munitions factory there. All Japanese planes returned safely to their bases on both raids. A third bombing was conducted on

p. 291

October 21, destroying many important bridges one after another. On October 25, a fourth raid was carried out, Japanese naval air units scoring direct hits on the important Kungkuo Bridge across the upper reaches of the Mekong River between Shanyang and Paoshan, completely destroying it. The Commander-in-Chief of the Japanese Fleet in China Waters sent a message of congratulation to the commander of the naval air force on this splendid achievement.

On October 26, large Japanese naval air formations extended their flight to Lowing, in the western extremity of Yunnan Province near the Burma border, and attacked an airplane factory there, scoring direct hits which resulted in the complete destruction of the plant. Fires were started in several places within the factory compound and all Japanese planes returned safely to their bases. The raid was significant in that it was conducted by the naval air force over a long distance and over mountainous territory and also because the factory was one of the largest of its kind in China. Its loss must have been a severe blow to the Chungking régime.

Again on October 28 a naval air detachment visited the Salween River (Nuchiang) and effectively bombed the important bridge spanning it. Other crack units of the Japanese naval air force raided Kunming, bombing military targets there, including a powder magazine on the northeastern outskirts of the town. The next day another bombing expedition was carried out against the Burma Road. The Hweitung Bridge across the Salween River was bombed and completely destroyed, thus interrupting the Burma Route not only at the Mekong River but also on the Salween River. The same day another naval air unit made a surprise attack on Chanyi, key point on the highway between Kunming and Kweiyang, capital of Kweichow Province, about 60 miles northeast of Kunming. In the ensuing air battle, the Japanese shot down one Chinese plane and destroyed another on the ground.

Messages of congratulation on its splendid achievements were sent to the naval air arm by H. I. H. Fleet-Admiral Prince Hiroyasu Fushimi, Chief of the Naval General Staff, Admiral Koshiro Oikawa, the Navy Minister, Admiral Shigetaro Shimada, Commander-in-Chief of the Japanese Fleet in China Waters, and General Gen Sugiyama, Chief of the Army General Staff.

Thus the Burma Route, on which the Chiang Kai-shek régime as well as Great Britain and the United States pinned their last hopes, has been smashed by the Japanese naval air arm. The Chungking régime apparently is making frantic efforts to repair the destroyed bridges, but the Japanese naval air force will repeat its bombings again and again whenever the route is reopened to traffic.
